title: Origin of the Visayan People: Srivijaya & Borneo Bisaya Ties
author: Glenn Junsay Pansensoy
excerpt: Trace Visayan origins from Austronesian roots through Srivijaya trade links and Borneo Bisaya connections.
body: Back to Home Hello and good day to everyone out there, welcome back, and this is another essay about the origin of the Visayan people and their connections to the Srivijaya Empire and to the Bisaya of Borneo. By Glenn Junsay Pansensoy (@PoeticGlenn) Published Feb 10, 2026 22 min read 📖 Introduction 🚢 Austronesian Roots 🏷️ The Name "Bisaya" 🗺️ Bisaya of Borneo 🌴 Early Society 🌊 Srivijaya Empire ⚓ Trade and Evidence 🔄 Cultural Exchange 🏁 Conclusion 📖 Introduction Hello and good day to everyone out there, welcome back, and this is another essay about the origin of the Visayan people and their connections to the Srivijaya Empire and to the Bisaya of Borneo. Today we are going to travel across the sea, back through centuries of migration, trade, and storytelling, to ask where the Visayans came from and how their history ties into the wider world of Maritime Southeast Asia. The Visayan people, known among themselves as Bisaya, form the largest ethnolinguistic group in the Philippines. They live across the central islands of the archipelago, the Visayas, and they have also settled widely in Mindanao and in other regions. Numbering in the tens of millions today, they speak a cluster of closely related languages, including Cebuano, Hiligaynon (Ilonggo), Waray, Kinaray-a, Aklanon, and several others. Many Filipinos in the diaspora carry these languages with them to every corner of the world. Their history is deeply rooted in the maritime world of Island Southeast Asia. To understand their origins, we have to look at four things at once: ancient population movements, the growth of language families, the trade networks that linked islands to empires, and the way later generations have interpreted that past through both scholarly research and popular tradition. In this essay we will follow six questions. Where did the earliest ancestors come from? What does the name "Bisaya" really mean? Is there a historical link to the Bisaya of Borneo, and what is the Maragtas? How far did the empire of Srivijaya reach? What evidence do we actually have for contact? And finally, what should we make of all of this today? Take it slowly, because the honest answer to many of these questions is more interesting than the legend. 🚢 Austronesian Foundations The deepest layer of Visayan origins belongs to the great Austronesian expansion. Beginning roughly four to five thousand years ago, seafaring farmers who spoke early forms of Austronesian languages moved out of Taiwan and into the northern Philippines. Archaeology in the Batanes islands and in northern Luzon shows these voyagers arriving with pottery, polished stone tools, domesticated animals, and an extraordinary skill in sailing. From the north they spread southward through the island chains, eventually reaching the rest of Maritime Southeast Asia, then Madagascar in the west and the distant islands of the Pacific in the east. It is one of the largest migrations in human history, and the Philippines sat near its starting point. The ancestors of the Visayans were part of this movement, and they met, mixed with, and learned from the older populations already living in the islands, such as the ancestors of today's Ati and other Negrito groups. By the time these communities settled the central Philippine islands, they already possessed sophisticated boat-building skills, navigational knowledge drawn from stars, winds, and currents, and a mixed economy based on fishing, hunting, gathering, and the cultivation of root crops and early forms of rice. The remains of ancient plank boats found in Butuan, in northern Mindanao, show how advanced this tradition was. Boats like these were the highways of the Visayan world. Over centuries these communities developed distinctive local cultures while staying connected to their neighbors through intermarriage, trade, and the exchange of ideas. Archaeological evidence from the Visayas shows continuous human presence for thousands of years. Shell middens, pottery styles, and burial practices reveal a gradual change from coastal foraging societies toward more settled agricultural villages. The spread of wet-rice farming, along with the raising of pigs, chickens, and water buffalo, supported growing populations and more complex social organization. Linguistically, the Visayan languages form a well-defined subgroup within the larger Philippine branch of Austronesian. They share distinctive vocabulary, sound changes, and grammatical features that set them apart from the languages of northern Luzon while still showing clear relationships to them. This unity points to a long period of shared development in the central islands, rather than a recent large-scale arrival of people from outside the Philippines. 🌴 Society and Belief By the first millennium of the Common Era, Visayan societies were organized around river mouths, sheltered bays, and fertile inland valleys. These settlements are often called barangay, a word that originally referred to the boat that carried a family or kin group. Leadership rested with datus, who commanded the loyalty of free warriors known as timawa and oversaw households of dependents, often called oripun. Rank was never fixed forever; a datu had to keep his following through generosity, courage, and success in trade and war. Status was displayed through gold ornaments, finely woven textiles, and elaborate tattooing. The Spanish who arrived in the sixteenth century were struck by the full-body tattoos of many Visayan men and called them Pintados, the painted ones. These tattoos recorded personal achievements, especially in warfare and raiding, and served as marks of identity and rank. When Magellan reached the central islands in 1521, and when Legazpi arrived in Cebu in 1565, they entered a world that was already busy, wealthy, and well connected. Religious life centered on a rich animist and ancestral tradition. People recognized a supreme creator figure in some areas, but daily practice focused on a multitude of spirits associated with the sea, forests, rice fields, and deceased relatives. Ritual specialists, often women known as babaylan, mediated between the human and spirit worlds through offerings, trance, and the recitation of long narrative poems. This spiritual framework would later absorb selective elements from Indianized cultures that reached the islands through trade, yet it remained fundamentally local in character. Why does this matter for the question of origins? Because it shows that Visayan society was not an empty land waiting for outside settlers. It was a mature, self-governing, maritime culture with its own institutions, long before any empire or colonial power wrote about it. 🏷️ The Name Bisaya The word "Bisaya" or "Visaya" itself has an uncertain etymology, and the debates over its origin have shaped how people understand Visayan identity. Early Spanish accounts used the term mainly for the inhabitants of Panay and nearby islands, distinguishing them from the tattooed populations of Cebu, Bohol, and Leyte, whom they continued to call Pintados. Over time the name expanded to cover the wider cluster of related peoples. One of the most persistent theories links the name to the great maritime empire of Srivijaya. In this view, "Bisaya" is a local transformation of the Sanskrit word vijaya, meaning victory, which appears in the empire's name Śrīvijaya. The idea gained popularity in the twentieth century because it connected the Visayans to a prestigious classical civilization. Yet linguistic analysis raises serious difficulties. The regular sound changes that carry Sanskrit and Old Malay words into Philippine languages would be expected to produce something closer to "Bidaya" or "Biraya", not "Bisaya". Other suggestions have been offered. Some scholars point to the Sanskrit term viṣaya, which means domain, territory, or sphere of influence. This could have been applied to a region or a group of polities. Still others propose purely local Austronesian roots whose original meanings have been lost. Chinese records from the Song dynasty, including the thirteenth-century account of Zhao Rugua, mention a people called "Pi-sho-ye" who raided the southern Chinese coast. Some researchers have wondered whether this is an early transcription of "Bisaya", though the identification remains uncertain, and the people described may not have been Visayans of the Philippines at all. What is clear is that by the time of Spanish colonization the name had become an important marker of identity for the peoples of the central Philippines. It distinguished them from the indigenous Ati of the interior and from the peoples of Luzon and Mindanao. In later centuries it became a source of regional pride, and the continuing debate over its origin reflects a broader question: how do Visayans locate themselves within the wider history of Southeast Asia? 🗺️ Bisaya of Borneo Across the Sulu Sea and the wider waters of northern Borneo lives another people who also call themselves Bisaya or Bisayah. They are found mainly in the Malaysian states of Sabah and Sarawak and in parts of Brunei. Historically they have been riverine farmers, cultivating rice, sago, and other crops along the lower reaches of major rivers, and many are known for their traditional buffalo-keeping and for their annual rice rituals. Their languages belong to the Austronesian family and show affinities with other northern Bornean groups. The existence of two peoples sharing the same name, separated by hundreds of kilometers of sea, has naturally invited speculation about a historical connection. The most famous expression of that idea is the Maragtas, a traditional narrative associated especially with the island of Panay. According to the story, in the thirteenth century ten datus led by Datu Puti fled the oppressive rule of a Bornean ruler named Makatunaw and sailed northward with their followers. Upon reaching Panay they negotiated with the local Ati, led by Marikudo, purchasing the lowlands in exchange for gold and other goods. The newcomers established settlements that became the foundation of later Visayan society in the western Visayas. The story is retold every year in festivals such as the Ati-Atihan of Kalibo, the Dinagyang of Iloilo, and the Binirayan of Antique. Despite its cultural importance, the Maragtas does not stand up well as a literal historical record. The best known written version was compiled by Pedro Alcantara Monteclaro and published in 1907, drawing on earlier oral and written material. Later historians, most famously William Henry Scott, examined its sources and concluded that parts of it rest on unreliable or even fabricated documents. Modern scholarship therefore regards it primarily as a later literary and oral tradition that crystallizes older memories of migration, alliance, and cultural encounter. Linguistic comparison between the Bisaya languages of Borneo and the Visayan languages of the Philippines reveals no especially close relationship beyond the general ties that connect all Austronesian languages of the region. Archaeology likewise shows continuous local development in the Visayas, not a sudden influx of Bornean settlers in the thirteenth century. Nevertheless, the story continues to hold meaning. It expresses a sense of connection to the wider Malay world and provides a dramatic origin narrative that elevates Visayan identity. In this sense the Maragtas functions more as a cultural charter than as a precise chronicle. It also carries a thoughtful moral: the ten datus buy the land rather than seizing it, and the Ati are remembered as the first people of the island. It reminds listeners that the Visayas have long been part of a maritime realm in which people, goods, and stories moved freely across the seas. 🌊 Srivijaya Empire To understand possible links between the Visayas and the classical empires of Island Southeast Asia, we must turn to Srivijaya itself. Emerging in the seventh century, with an early inscription dated 683 and its center near present-day Palembang on the island of Sumatra, Srivijaya grew into the dominant maritime power of the western Indonesian archipelago. Its strength rested on control of the Strait of Malacca and other vital sea lanes that carried spices, aromatic woods, gold, tin, textiles, and ceramics between China, India, and the Middle East. Srivijaya was a thalassocracy, an empire of the sea rather than a vast territorial state. Its rulers exercised authority through a combination of naval power, commercial monopolies, diplomatic alliances, and the prestige of Mahayana Buddhism. Chinese pilgrims traveling to India often stopped in Srivijaya to study Buddhist texts, and the empire maintained monasteries and scholarly contacts that reached as far as the Indian subcontinent. At various times its influence extended over parts of the Malay Peninsula, western Java, and coastal Borneo. Direct political control over the Philippine islands is not documented in the surviving records of Srivijaya. The empire's known tributaries and dependencies do not include the Visayas. Yet the Philippines clearly took part in the same maritime trading networks. Goods and ideas moved along routes that linked the South China Sea with the Java Sea and the Strait of Malacca, and cultural influences from the Indianized kingdoms of Sumatra and the Malay world reached Philippine shores. One of the most important pieces of evidence is the Laguna Copperplate Inscription, discovered in Luzon and dated to the year 900. Written in a mixture of Old Malay with Sanskrit and some Old Javanese and Old Tagalog terms, it records the clearing of a debt and mentions a place called Sribuza, widely understood as a reference to Srivijaya. The document shows that by the early tenth century at least some Philippine polities were familiar with the political and commercial world centered on Sumatra and used related legal and administrative concepts. Archaeological finds in the Visayas and neighboring areas further illustrate these connections. Chinese ceramics of Tang and Song date appear in coastal sites, as do gold ornaments whose styles show affinities with objects found across Maritime Southeast Asia. The golden Tara image from Agusan, in northern Mindanao, reflects Hindu-Buddhist artistic influence. Certain forms of jewelry, including the distinctive lingling-o earrings, occur in both Philippine and Indonesian contexts. Indianized titles such as raja appear alongside the indigenous term datu, suggesting that local leaders sometimes adopted foreign symbols of authority to enhance their prestige. These contacts were real and significant, yet they do not support the stronger claim that the Visayan people themselves originated as colonists from Srivijaya, or that the islands formed a formal province of the empire. The evidence points instead to participation in a shared maritime world in which influence flowed through trade, intermarriage among elites, and the selective adoption of prestigious foreign practices. When Srivijaya declined under pressure from the Chola dynasty of South India in the eleventh century and later from rising Javanese powers, the commercial networks it had dominated did not disappear; they reorganized under new centers, and Philippine communities kept trading and absorbing new influences from the evolving Malay and Javanese worlds. ⚓ Trade and Evidence If we want to judge any theory of origin, it helps to ask what kinds of evidence exist and what each one can prove. There are at least four kinds: archaeology, linguistics, written records, and oral tradition. Each answers different questions, and each has limits. Archaeology tells us what people made, ate, traded, and buried with their dead. For the Visayas, it shows long continuity and steady outside contact, but not a single moment of mass arrival from Sumatra or Borneo. Linguistics tells us how languages are related. The Visayan languages sit firmly inside the Philippine branch of Austronesian, and borrowed words from Sanskrit and Malay, such as words for religion, rank, and trade goods, show contact rather than replacement. A language shift of the kind that a mass migration would cause is simply not visible. Written records are precious but late and partial. Chinese sources describe trade and raiding along the southern coasts, the Laguna Copperplate Inscription provides a rare local document, and Spanish chroniclers describe the Visayas as they were in the sixteenth century. None of them records a Srivijayan conquest of the Visayas. Oral tradition, including epics and the Maragtas, preserves values, memories, and identities, but it is shaped by the needs of each generation that retells it. Taken together, these sources form a consistent picture. The Visayans are an Austronesian people with deep local roots, active in the trade of their time, and open to ideas from Sumatra, Java, India, and China. Genetic studies of Southeast Asian populations point in the same direction, showing that Filipino groups carry a mix of ancient Austronesian ancestry and older local lineages, though such studies are still developing and are best read with care. 🔄 Cultural Exchange The cumulative effect of centuries of maritime interaction shaped Visayan culture in subtle but lasting ways. Boat design, navigational techniques, and the vocabulary of trade show connections across the region. Certain social institutions, such as the elevated status of datus and the use of gold as a measure of wealth and rank, parallel practices found in other Austronesian societies influenced by Indianized models. At the same time, the core of Visayan life, meaning language, kinship, local religion, and agricultural practices, remained distinctly Philippine. After Spanish colonization began in the sixteenth century, Visayan identity was reshaped again. Christianity spread, towns were reorganized around the church plaza, and the old tattooing and many ritual practices faded. Yet memory survived in songs, epics, festivals, and family stories. The Ati-Atihan, with its painted faces, drums, and dancing, is a good example of how older and newer layers of culture can live side by side. In the modern era, the desire to place Visayan history within a broader Southeast Asian framework has kept the Srivijaya and Borneo theories alive in the popular imagination. School textbooks of earlier generations sometimes presented a simplified narrative of waves of migration from the south. Festival pageantry continues to dramatize the arrival of the ten datus. These stories serve important social functions: they foster regional pride, create a sense of historical depth, and link local identity to the classical civilizations of the Malay world. Scholarly research, by contrast, emphasizes continuity and local development while acknowledging the reality of long-distance contacts. The Visayans are best understood as an Austronesian people who settled the central Philippines in ancient times, developed their own societies over many centuries, and took part actively in the commercial and cultural exchanges that characterized pre-modern Southeast Asia. Their relationship to Srivijaya was one of indirect influence through shared trade routes, not direct descent or political subordination. Their relationship to the Bisaya of Borneo is one of parallel naming and possible distant common heritage within the Austronesian family, not of recent colonization in either direction. 🏁 Conclusion This more measured view does not diminish the richness of Visayan history. On the contrary, it places the Visayans firmly within one of the great maritime cultural zones of the world, a zone defined by movement, exchange, and creative adaptation. From the first Austronesian settlers who brought language and technology to the islands, through the centuries of trade that linked them to Sumatra, China, and India, to the complex societies encountered by the Spanish, the Visayan people have been active participants in the making of Southeast Asian civilization. So what should you take away from this essay? First, the Visayans descend mainly from Austronesian settlers who made the central Philippines their home thousands of years ago. Second, the name Bisaya is still an open question, and the Srivijaya explanation, though popular, has real linguistic problems. Third, the Maragtas is a treasured tradition, but it should be read as cultural memory rather than as a literal record. Fourth, trade and cultural contact with Srivijaya and the Malay world were real, but they were not conquest or colonization. And finally, the best history is the kind that stays honest about what we know and what we do not. Thank you for listening and for reading. If you enjoyed this essay, please share it with a friend who loves history, and come back for the next one. Until then, good day to everyone out there. "The Visayan story is not one of simple origin from a single foreign source, but of deep local roots enriched by centuries of connection across the sea."
